content: The Delphi-like consultation revealed that there was only a 52% agreement on the specified cost of the instrument. Public comments indicated that the initial cost range of USD 1,000 for minimal requirements was unrealistic, with suggestions for a broader range between USD 3,000 and USD 7,000. The group acknowledged the difficulty in determining an appropriate cost range, emphasizing its dependence on factors such as volume, consumables, and operational considerations. These factors were incorporated into the revised capital cost for the instrument under minimal requirements. In January 2021, the WHO initiated an online public comment process to finalize the revised Target Product Profile (TPP) document for tuberculosis (TB) diagnostic tests and drug resistance detection. This process aimed to ensure that proposed changes were objective and balanced, considering the needs and values of patients, end users, and industry stakeholders. Stakeholders were invited to provide feedback on the scope, target users or settings, pricing, test performance, and operational characteristics. A total of 128 individuals accessed the call for public comment, with 82 agreeing to participate. The distribution of responses by sector is detailed in Figure 1. The survey comments generally aligned with the proposed TPP, with most being relatively minor. However, divergent views were expressed in specific areas, including prioritizing new drugs like pyrazinamide (PZA) due to its role in many regimens, expanding the target population to include children with pediatric-friendly samples such as stool, and lowering pricing criteria to more realistic levels for low-income countries. Specific comments on diagnostic performance also required attention. Regarding the scope, five respondents emphasized the importance of PZA, particularly for people living with HIV. One respondent suggested that the optimal requirements should include bedaquiline (BDQ), linezolid (LZD), clofazimine (CFZ), and PZA. Two respondents proposed replacing CFZ with pretomanid (Pa) in the optimal second level, while three suggested adding Pa to the regimen. One respondent recommended including delamanid (DLM) with BDQ, LZD, and CFZ in the optimal second level due to its role in shortened pediatric regimens, while another suggested adding D-cycloserine to the optimal third level. For minimal requirements, one respondent stated that the first level should include fluoroquinolones (FQ), while four respondents suggested replacing amikacin (AMK) with BDQ ± LZD in the third level. One respondent emphasized the inclusion of BDQ and CFZ, with or without LZD. For the target population, four respondents advocated for expanding it to include children, noting that stool works well as a sample. Five respondents suggested including stool and other WHO-recommended extrapulmonary samples in explanatory notes. In terms of performance characteristics, three respondents recommended changing the optimal limit of detection to 10 colony-forming units (CFU)/mL to align with Xpert® MTB/RIF Ultra (Xpert Ultra). One respondent noted that a limit of detection of 10^4 is too high for many people living with HIV. Sensitivity criteria for TB detection were generally seen as too low, with respondents emphasizing that sensitivity should match or exceed Xpert Ultra, particularly in smear-negative cases. One respondent suggested that the minimal smear-positive sensitivity should be at least 95%. For drug-susceptibility testing (DST), sensitivity compared to a sequencing reference standard will vary by drug, making a uniform requirement unrealistic. Compared to a phenotypic reference standard, DST sensitivity of more than 95% for all drugs is likely unfeasible; instead, targets should be updated as genetic information becomes available. Exceptionally, rifampicin (RIF) sensitivity should exceed 98%, and PZA minimal sensitivity should exceed 90%. Specificity criteria for DST should account for composite reference standards (phenotypic and sequencing combined). Analytical specificity for non-tuberculous mycobacteria was both appreciated and questioned by respondents. The optimal limit of detection for minor variants should decrease to 1%, aligning with the mycobacterial growth indicator tube (MGIT™), and to less than 5% for minimal requirements, as this is critical for understanding treatment success. Regarding indeterminate DST results, one respondent suggested reducing the optimal value to less than 1%, while another believed such stringent values could hinder test development. One respondent proposed distinct values for smear-positive and smear-negative cases. Three respondents recommended reducing reproducibility criteria to less than 5%. Operational characteristics raised concerns about high costs if daily throughput is low. Five respondents suggested specifying distinct options for lowand high-incidence settings. The definition of optimal throughput should decrease to 10 tests or fewer, while minimal should change to 11–25 tests. Three implementing partner respondents opposed batching due to concerns about delays in testing. Pricing was considered too high for lowand middle-income countries (LMICs) by six respondents from academia, advocacy, implementing partners, and industry. Pricing should be based on the cost of goods sold and volume, not on the ability to pay or perceived value. Suggested minimal prices for RIF and isoniazid (INH) ranged from USD 10–15 (advocacy) to USD 18–25 (industry). Suggested optimal prices for RIF/INH were less than USD 5 (advocacy and industry). For RIF/INH/FQ/AMK, optimal pricing suggestions were less than USD 10 (advocacy and industry) and USD 15–20 (industry). One industry respondent disagreed with setting minimum prices, arguing that it could stifle innovation. Another advocacy respondent stated that basing non-culture DST pricing on culture is unreasonable and suggested using the cost of existing molecular tests instead. Four respondents emphasized the need to reduce instrument costs, and three highlighted the importance of prioritizing generic or universal instruments requiring minimal updates. New service and delivery models, such as reagent rental models, were suggested to spread costs over a large volume of tests. One industry respondent noted that individual test costs are unrealistically low, while equipment, maintenance, and warranty costs are unrealistically high. Respondents also raised concerns about operational feasibility. One respondent suggested that instruments should function in non-air-conditioned environments, while another emphasized the need for resistance to high levels of ambient dust. Minimal battery power should last 24 hours. Turnaround time should decrease, with a goal of a rapid test format suitable for point-of-care (POC) or bedside use. Five respondents considered the minimal time to results too long, suggesting times of 4–6 hours (one respondent) and less than 2 hours (three respondents). Optimal timing should decrease to less than 30 minutes. Maintenance should be inexpensive, achievable by local staff, and included in equipment costs. Equipment manufacturers should have at least one support person available in each WHO region. However, one respondent believed these criteria were unrealistic. Regarding training, three respondents suggested reducing the minimal training time to two days or less, and one highlighted the need for training on maintenance and software updates. Four respondents expressed a preference for reusable, recyclable, or non-plastic alternatives to disposables. One respondent proposed aligning biosafety and waste disposal requirements with those of rapid molecular tests rather than microscopy. Another suggested adding a data export criterion for reporting results to clients, while two respondents recommended including requirements for virus or malware protection and data security.
